text: Why do people stay in New York even while it's quietly making them broke? median rent in Manhattan just hit around $5,000 a month, half a paycheck gone, before food, and still nobody leaves. That isn't stubbornness. It's a bet, and the bet has a name. In 1890, an economist named Alfred Marshall noticed something strange about cities. Pack people doing similar work close together, and each one becomes more productive than they be alone. He called it a glamoration. A century later, Harvard's Edward Glazer proved it holds. Workers in dense cities earn more, learn faster, and produce more, and the effect grows the tighter you pack them. Proximity isn't a nice to have. It compounds. So here's what that $5,000 actually buys. Not an apartment. Proximity. You're paying for the room. The chance hallway conversation. The friend of a friend who runs a fund. The intro that skips five years of grinding. New York has more wealthy investors per square mile than almost anywhere on earth. Half a million college students feeding in every year, and the highest concentration of major buyers in the country. You're not renting a place to sleep. You're renting access to collisions. And there's a quieter engine. Surround yourself with people working brutally hard, and it drags your own baseline up. Ambition is contagious. Effort spreads like a virus. In New York, the whole city has the fever. So you catch it whether you meant to or not. But here's what nobody says. Proximity is not the same as success. And the city knows exactly what proximity is worth, which is why it prices your rent to swallow it. You pay the premium upfront, guaranteed every month. The upside only pays out for a few. So most people go broke funding a lottery. And the landlord collects whether or not your number ever comes up. The city sells the ticket. It never promised the prize. So why stay broke? Because leaving feels like folding the hand right before the last card. The fear was never the rent. It's that the one encounter that would have changed everything happens the week after you give up and move home. That fear is the most valuable thing New York sells. It doesn't rent you an apartment. It rents you the version of yourself you might still become. And it charges you everything you have to keep you at the table.
